title: A home for unfinished ideas
description: Building Firelink Chronicle — a small, thoughtful home for projects, notes, and discoveries.
text: The idea # Firelink Chronicle brings three kinds of work together: things being built, things being learned, and things worth exploring. The intention is to leave a useful trail rather than wait until every idea feels finished. The visual language borrows its atmosphere from Dark Souls and Elden Ring : weathered stone, old gold, distant landscapes, and a little light against the dark. The writing stays direct and readable. Four places to begin # The Wanderer introduces the person behind the pages. The Forge holds projects, decisions, and things made along the way. The Archives keeps learning notes that can be returned to later. Beyond the Fog is for questions, observations, and discoveries without a fixed destination. What this project includes # Each entry has its own address, tags, reading time, and table of contents. The collection can be browsed by section, tag, or date. Search covers titles, summaries, and the full text of entries. An RSS feed offers a quieter way to follow updates. The site is static and hosted on GitHub Pages. Its content lives in Markdown, with a small build script producing the pages and indexes. What comes next # The foundation is ready. The next step is to replace the starter entries with personal work and let the site grow from there. New features should earn their place by making writing or reading easier. A small beginning is still a beginning. Explore the source on GitHub .

title: Leave a trail while learning
description: A simple structure for notes that preserve the question, the experiment, and what changed.
text: Begin with a question # A useful learning note does not need to cover an entire subject. Start with the thing that was unclear. A precise question gives the note a reason to exist and makes it easier to find again. For example: Why does this approach work here, and when would it stop working? Keep the experiment small # Write down one attempt. Include the minimum example that explains the result, and distinguish what was observed from what is still a guess. Question: What am I trying to understand? Attempt: What did I try? Observation: What actually happened? Next step: What should I investigate next? Record what changed # The most valuable part of a note is often the difference between the first assumption and the final understanding. Preserve that change. It is a better reminder than a polished definition alone. Keep the original question visible. Record errors that explain a mistaken assumption. Link to the source that helped. Leave an explicit next question when the answer is incomplete. Return to the trail # Give the note a descriptive title and a few specific tags. Revisit it when a related problem appears. A growing archive should be a working companion, not a shelf that is never opened. This is a starter entry demonstrating the learning-note layout. Replace it with a real question from your own work.

title: The value of an unmarked path
description: A starting point for exploring atmosphere, curiosity, and the questions a world leaves unanswered.
text: An invitation to look closer # Some worlds invite us to move slowly. A distant shape, a quiet doorway, or a fragment of architecture can be enough to turn a walk into a question. The appeal of a dark fantasy landscape is not only its scale. It is the feeling that the place continues beyond what can be explained at first glance. Atmosphere as a starting point # Darkness, texture, and silence can make small details feel significant. For this blog, that atmosphere becomes a setting for writing: an old-gold accent, a restrained illustration, and enough space for the words to breathe. The design should invite exploration without making the reader work to understand the navigation. Questions worth keeping # What makes a place feel like it has a history? How much can a detail suggest without explaining everything? When does uncertainty encourage curiosity, and when does it become friction? These are prompts for exploration, not conclusions. A good entry in this section can begin with a question and end with a better one. Carry something back # Curiosity becomes more useful when it leaves a trace: an observation, a sketch, a link, or a short paragraph. The discovery does not have to be large enough for a finished essay. This is a starter entry demonstrating the exploration layout. Replace it with your own observations, reading, or game experiences.
